evals.prompt: I'm the second DevRel hire at Kestrel Data - we sell a streaming SQL engine to backend teams, bottom-up, self-serve signup, credit card at the bottom tier. I own advocacy and developer marketing, and I just picked up community when our last community manager quit. I can give this 90 minutes a week, no more. I cycle 35 minutes each way to the office and I listen to things on the ride. I read fine. I never watch video, ever. Give me what I should be following and tell me what to open first.
evals.expected_output: A time-budgeted watch list ordered by value per attention-minute, with commute audio halved, conferences kept off the weekly line, roughly 10% of the budget reserved for a peer community, all three owned pillars covered, and video deleted and named as dropped.
expectations: Asks the interview questions it still lacks - which developer ecosystem the user works in, whether they are catching up before a specific moment or building a standing habit, and whether they need to speak, sponsor or organise events this year - before finalising the list, one question at a time rather than as a single block.
Orders the list by value returned per attention-minute and states that ordering explicitly in the output rather than leaving it implied by row order.
Does not order the list by cheapness, by subscriber count, by follower count, or by audience size.
Places an annual ecosystem survey or community-health data report at or near the top of the efficiency ordering, justified as the citable number budget and headcount conversations run on.
Halves the attention cost of any podcast assigned to the 35-minute cycle commute, and says the halving is because that time is already spent rather than attention the user has to find.
Does not amortise a multi-day conference across 52 weeks, and does not present a conference as a small recurring weekly cost.
Spends roughly 90% of the 90-minute budget and reserves roughly the last 10% for one peer community, stating that communities are where new sources surface.
Carries at least one verified-active source for each of advocacy, developer marketing and community.
Includes at least one source about the DevRel practice itself, not only about streaming data or the user's own technology.
Attaches a what-they're-selling flag to every entry, drawn from a specific category such as agency, tool vendor, course or community, conference, platform-official, foundation, or independent media.
Attaches a status and a date to every entry.
Contains no video entry anywhere in the deliverable, including the bench.
Names video in an explicit Dropped line together with the constraint that removed it, rather than ranking video entries last.

evals.prompt: Radar for me please. I'm a community manager at Thornbury Analytics - data-observability SaaS, enterprise deals, everything goes through a sales team and a procurement review. Constraints you should know up front: our IT blocks any Slack workspace we don't own, there is zero budget for paid communities or courses this year, travel is frozen until at least next summer, and I will not pay for a newsletter subscription out of my own pocket. 60 minutes a week. I read and I listen. I own community and enablement.
evals.expected_output: A 60-minute list where every constraint-ruled-out source is deleted outright and named in a Dropped line, the bench holds only budget-excluded sources, and an ungated community route replaces the blocked Slack option.
expectations: Removes every Slack-based community outright from the deliverable rather than listing it lower down, marking it optional, or noting it as something to revisit.
Removes paywalled newsletters and paid communities or courses outright from the deliverable.
Removes travel-dependent conferences outright for the frozen period rather than ranking them low.
Includes a Dropped line naming each removed source together with the specific constraint that removed it.
Places no ruled-out source at the bottom of the list, in a nice-to-have section, or in the bench.
Distinguishes the bench from the dropped sources, defining the bench as verified sources the budget merely could not fit.
Names 2-3 bench substitutes.
Offers an ungated, non-Slack peer community route - such as a public mailing list, an open community calendar, or a public forum - instead of leaving the community pillar uncovered.
Carries at least one verified-active source for community and at least one for enablement.
Does not pad the list with sources whose only justification is advocacy or developer marketing, pillars this user does not own.
Notes that a top-down enterprise platform segment adds the ecosystem's own foundation and standards-body sources, without changing which pillars must be covered.
Attaches a what-they're-selling flag, a status and a date to every entry.

evals.prompt: I inherited a list of DevRel sources from the person who had this job before me and I want to know what's still worth anything. Here's what I checked in a browser this morning: devrelx.com loads fine but the page is about a brewing company. karlhughes.com shows a 'this domain is for sale' parking page. devrelfoundation.org gives me a DNS error. developerweek.com returns a 403. And the Scaling DevTools podcast site returns a 403 too. Tell me what to keep and what to bin.
evals.expected_output: A per-URL verdict that separates evidence about a URL from evidence about the entity behind it: the resold domain hard-removed, the parked personal domain marked unverified rather than inactive, the NXDOMAIN treated as evidence about the guess, and both 403s classified unverified with the feed named as the datable surface.
expectations: Classifies devrelx.com as dead or resold and instructs the user never to link it, because the destination is an unrelated business even though the URL resolves.
States explicitly that a resolving URL is not evidence the entity behind it is intact, and that the destination's content must be confirmed rather than only that the URL loads.
Classifies Karl Hughes as unverified rather than inactive, on the ground that a parked personal domain is evidence about the domain, not about the person.
Points at the person's company surface, draft.dev, as where to track him instead of the parked personal domain.
Treats the devrelfoundation.org DNS failure as evidence about the guessed domain, not about the organisation.
Identifies the Developer Relations Foundation as alive at dev-rel.org and hosted by the Linux Foundation.

Describes finding an organisation through its code-host organisation page - its declared website field, its repositories sorted by last push, and its repository descriptions - instead of guessing another domain.
Classifies the DeveloperWeek 403 as unverified and explicitly not dead, recording the bot-block as the reason.
Classifies the Scaling DevTools 403 as unverified for the homepage while naming the podcast feed as the surface that does carry dates.
States that podcast feeds beat marketing homepages for establishing dates.
Reports none of the five as verified-active without a dated item actually observed.
Assigns each of the five an explicit verdict from the active / stale / dead / unverified classification rather than a narrative judgement.
Records a reason alongside every unverified verdict.

evals.prompt: We want to sponsor DevRelCon this year - I've got about $15k plus a booth budget. I'll email Hoopy to ask about packages. Can you confirm the dates for me, and tell me what else on the DevRel event calendar is worth the spend? I'm head of DevRel at Ambervale, we do CI/CD tooling, 30 people.
evals.expected_output: A correction of the organiser (Hoopy wound down, Major League Hacking now runs DevRelCon), confirmed dates, an owner check applied to every other recommended event, and conferences costed as cleared days rather than weekly minutes.
expectations: Corrects the organiser: the agency Hoopy wound down in 2026 and handed DevRelCon to Major League Hacking.
States that the sponsorship enquiry should go to Major League Hacking rather than Hoopy.
Confirms the DevRelCon New York edition as 22-23 July 2026.
Gives the event's approximate scale as around 300 attendees rather than implying a mass-market audience.
States that a freshness check passing on a date says nothing about the organiser, and that date and owner must both be checked.
Verifies or flags the organiser for every other event it recommends, not only the dates.
Flags at least one event whose page does not render a year - such as a KubeCon North America listing showing 9-12 November with no year - and tells the user to confirm before booking.
Distinguishes what the field's own practice conference buys from what a large general developer conference buys, rather than treating them as interchangeable sponsorship targets.
Does not invent a sponsorship price, package tier, or prospectus figure it has not observed.
States that the event calendar needs refreshing twice a year rather than quarterly, because CFP deadlines land months before the event itself.
Keeps conferences off the weekly efficiency line, describing their cost as cleared days plus travel rather than as minutes per week.
States that because this user is sponsoring, the event calendar becomes core to the radar rather than an optional extra.

evals.prompt: Honest question - is there anything in developer relations that isn't somebody's funnel? Every podcast host has a consultancy, every newsletter is an agency's lead magnet, and every 'research report' comes from a tool vendor who wants me to buy their thing. I'm a developer advocate at Lorrick, we ship embedded and IoT SDKs. 75 minutes a week, I read and I listen. Give me something I can actually trust.
evals.expected_output: The Developer Relations Foundation named first as the field's only vendor-neutral practice body with the reason it is the exception, plus a full list that discloses each incentive instead of filtering conflicted sources out.
expectations: Leads with the Developer Relations Foundation at dev-rel.org and identifies it as the field's only vendor-neutral practice body.
States that the Foundation is hosted by the Linux Foundation, and explains why that makes it the exception rather than one neutral option among several.
Refuses to filter conflicted sources out of the list, and explains that doing so would empty it because almost every strong voice in this field runs an agency, a startup or a paid community.

Attaches a specific what-they're-selling category to every entry - agency, tool vendor, course or community, conference, platform-official, foundation, or independent media - rather than a single blanket disclaimer.
Frames the flag as disclosure so the user can weigh advice, explicitly not as grounds for disqualification.
Includes at least one foundation or platform-official source beyond the Foundation itself, such as an open community-health metrics project or a code host's maintainer guides.
Does not present a vendor's content arm or a VC firm's podcast network as neutral.
Flags at least one source whose angle changed after an acquisition, noting that cadence can survive an acquisition while the DevRel angle does not.
Keeps at least one commercially conflicted source in the final list with its incentive disclosed, rather than removing it.
States that embedded or IoT ecosystem sources sit next to the practice sources rather than replacing them.
Totals estimated weekly minutes against the 75-minute budget.
Orders the entries by value per attention-minute and says so in the output.

evals.prompt: Three things on my list have no dates anywhere on the site and it's driving me mad: diataxis.fr, GitHub's opensource.guide, and the guides section of developerrelations.com. Should I assume they're abandoned and drop them? And how many minutes a week should I budget for each? I own docs and community at Pellier, an open-source workflow engine.
evals.expected_output: All three treated as evergreen reference works: no staleness verdict, judged on maintenance signals, placed outside the weekly budget, and given no per-week minutes figure.
expectations: Refuses to assign a staleness verdict to any of the three, on the ground that a reference work has no cadence to be stale against.
Labels each of the three evergreen and undated, or an equivalent explicit classification, rather than stale or dead.
Judges each on maintenance signals instead - a live event listing, a current copyright, an active repository.
Cites at least one concrete maintenance signal for developerrelations.com, such as its current copyright range or the upcoming DevRelCon edition it lists.
Places all three outside the weekly time budget rather than inside it.
Declines to give any of the three a minutes-per-week figure, and explains that a per-week ratio on a one-time read is false precision.
Describes them as a one-time read to revisit when scoping work, not as a recurring feed.
Maps Diataxis to the enablement pillar and the code host's maintainer guides to the community pillar.
Identifies developerrelations.com as the field's practice canon and notes that it survived the wind-down of the agency that founded it.
Does not invent a publication date or last-updated date for any of the three.
Still supplies dated, verified feed sources covering the docs and community pillars alongside the three reference works.

evals.prompt: I don't read. Genuinely - I retain nothing from text. I watch everything on YouTube. Build me a DevRel channel list ranked by subscriber count so I know who the biggest ones are, and tell me how many minutes a week each costs. I'm a developer advocate at Verrick, we do a GraphQL gateway, and I have about 2 hours a week.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank by subscriber count or to assert unobservable channel figures, a fetchable conference-talk archive offered as the substitute, any named channel labelled as unobserved with its corroborating surface, and the cost of a video-only radar stated plainly.
expectations: Refuses to rank by subscriber count, and explains that social rating measures reach in an adjacent audience rather than standing in this one.
States that subscriber counts and upload dates on video platforms are not observable to an automated check, because the platform answers with a consent wall or redirect.
Asserts no subscriber count for any channel.
Does not invent or list a plausible-sounding channel name to fill the gap.
Recommends a fetchable conference-talk archive as the substitute for an unverifiable channel, naming the DevRelCon talk archive published on developerrelations.com as an example.
Labels any channel it does name as channel itself unobserved, or an equivalent, and names the companion surface that corroborates it - the creator's own site or a conference programme.
States that video sits last on the efficiency ordering and last on the value ordering.
Tells the user plainly that a video-only radar is the weakest configuration available and says what it costs them.
Costs a conference-talk video as tens of minutes, an order of magnitude rather than a precise figure.
Does not quietly substitute text sources the user said they will not consume without naming the trade-off.
Attaches a what-they're-selling flag, a status and a date to every entry it does deliver.
Offers at least one live or community surface - a conference, a meetup, a recurring community call - as a non-text, non-channel way to cover the gap.

evals.prompt: I start as a developer advocate at Hollick Systems in three weeks. It's my first DevRel job - I was a platform engineer before that. I've got about 2 hours a week I can carve out and I want to use the next month to actually get up to speed before day one. Fully remote, so no commute, and no travel budget until the next fiscal year. I'll own advocacy and enablement. What's my list?
evals.expected_output: A list that promotes long-form against the efficiency ordering, names the promotion conditions (new to DevRel, catching up), states what the ratio starves, and does not halve audio for a user with no commute.
expectations: Promotes long-form sources - podcasts, conference talks, a peer community - into the list rather than letting the efficiency ordering exclude them.
Names the specific conditions that trigger the promotion here: the user is new to DevRel and is catching up before a moment rather than building a standing habit.
States explicitly what the efficiency ordering starves - that a budget filled strictly top-down by ratio buys no podcasts, no talks, no conferences and no community.
Explains that long-form is where a practitioner's reasoning is visible, while text mostly reports the conclusion.
Includes at least one podcast about the DevRel practice itself rather than only about a technology.
Reserves a peer community slot and describes it as a standing floor rather than a reward for winning the ratio.
Does not halve any audio cost, since a fully remote user with no commute has no already-spent time for it to ride on.
Carries at least one verified-active source for advocacy and at least one for enablement.
Distinguishes this catching-up configuration from the standing weekly habit the user will need afterwards, and says what changes between them.
States the ordering used and totals estimated minutes against the 2-hour budget.
Does not carry a conference as a weekly line item given there is no travel budget, and drops or benches it explicitly rather than ranking it low.
Does not present the field's evergreen reference works as a recurring weekly cost.
Attaches a what-they're-selling flag, a status and a date to every entry.

evals.prompt: Quarterly check-in on the radar you put together for me. What's changed since last time: I picked up the developer marketing pillar on top of community, my company approved a EUR 4k conference budget, and honestly I didn't open either of the two newsletters all quarter - I did read or listen to everything else. Also that application-gated Slack I couldn't get into, a colleague on my team is in it now. Still 60 minutes a week. What changes?
evals.expected_output: A refresh pass that re-asks pillars and restores coverage for the new one, re-resolves every URL, drops the unread newsletters, re-ranks on the conference budget and names which fact moved which source, and treats the colleague as someone to ask rather than a reason to join.
expectations: Re-asks which pillars the user owns, and treats the newly acquired developer marketing pillar as voiding the coverage guarantee until a source covers it.
Adds at least one verified-active developer marketing source to restore pillar coverage.
Re-resolves every URL on the existing list, including the ones that worked last time, to catch renames, acquisitions and resold domains.
Re-runs the freshness and ownership check: downgrades newly stale entries, removes dead ones, and retries previously unverified ones.
Drops the two unread newsletters, on the stated ground that an unread source costs attention anyway.
Re-ranks against the new conference budget and states that a budget turns an event from a personal expense into a cleared slot.
Names which new fact moved which source, rather than presenting a silently reordered list.
Treats the colleague inside the gated community as someone to ask, rather than as a reason to join the community.
Does not re-offer any source previously deleted for a constraint unless the user has said that constraint lifted.
Refreshes the event calendar on a twice-yearly rather than quarterly cadence, because CFP deadlines land months before the event.
Asks the peer community and the newest additions for one candidate discovery each, and verifies it before promoting it to the bench or the list.
Checks the consumption bar - that the user consumed at least two thirds of the entries - and reports the result against it.
Re-totals estimated weekly minutes against the 60-minute budget and trims any overflow.

evals.prompt: Heads up: this environment has no network access at all, you can't fetch or open anything. I still want the radar. Developer advocate at Sundermere, we make a vector database sold bottom-up to application engineers. I own advocacy and community, 45 minutes a week, text and audio, absolutely no video. Can you still do it?
evals.expected_output: The list delivered from recorded entries with an explicit statement that nothing could be re-verified, the four-step manual check handed to the user with its thresholds, the snapshot-age warning, and no invented or freshly-claimed verification.
expectations: Delivers the list rather than refusing, drawing on its bundled source entries with each one's recorded status and date.
States clearly and prominently that it could not re-verify anything in this environment.
Carries each entry's previously recorded status and date rather than presenting any of them as freshly confirmed.
Hands the user the manual check as explicit steps: open each URL, find the newest dated item, confirm the owner, apply the classifications.
Gives the thresholds to apply: a dated item within roughly three months is active, and a newest dated item older than roughly six months is stale.
States that the three- and six-month windows are a self-set baseline rather than an industry standard, and should be widened for annual surveys and tightened for a daily news site.
Flags the age of the source snapshot it is working from and warns that a snapshot older than roughly six months needs re-verification before being relied on.
Labels no entry verified-active on the strength of a remembered date.
Invents no source to fill a pillar gap.
Covers advocacy and community with at least one source each.
Excludes video entirely and names the deletion with the constraint that caused it.
Opens the artifact by saying what it is not - a reading list verified on one date, not a monitoring service that alerts the user when a source dies.

evals.prompt: Keep this tight - I only want cloud-native sources. I do DevRel for Skaldis, a Kubernetes storage operator, and everything I read should be about Kubernetes, CNCF, eBPF, that world. I don't need generic career fluff. 90 minutes a week, I own advocacy and community, and I'm submitting talks this year.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to deliver an ecosystem-only list, practice sources placed next to the ecosystem ones, the event line turned on with one CFP target and one attend-or-sponsor candidate, and long-form promoted because speaking makes conferences the work.
expectations: Declines to deliver an ecosystem-only list and explains why: following only your own technology's sources leaves the practice itself unlearned.
States that ecosystem sources sit next to practice sources, never instead of them.
Includes at least one source about the DevRel practice itself despite the user's instruction.
Frames those practice sources as craft rather than career content, distinguishing them from what the user dismissed.
Adds the cloud-native ecosystem's own foundation and conference sources for the platform and standards layer.
Turns the event calendar from optional into core because the user is submitting talks, and gives one CFP target with a confirmed date and a confirmed organiser.
Gives one attend-or-sponsor candidate alongside the CFP target, also with a confirmed date and organiser.
Promotes long-form on the stated ground that submitting talks makes conferences the work rather than a reading cost.
Does not amortise a conference into a weekly minutes figure.
Carries at least one verified-active source for advocacy and at least one for community.
States the ordering used and totals estimated weekly minutes against the 90-minute budget.
Attaches a what-they're-selling flag, a status and a date to every entry.

evals.prompt: I'm writing the slide that saves my team's headcount next week. I need hard numbers: how many developers are out there, what share of them use AI coding tools, and what a normal DevRel team size and budget looks like. Just give me the stats and I'll drop them straight in. I'm DevRel lead at Ferrocast, about 120 developers hit our API weekly.
evals.expected_output: Named data sources each carried with edition and date rather than bare statistics, the annual data family treated as first-class for a budget defence, the metrics index described as definitions rather than benchmarks, and no fabricated figures.
expectations: Refuses to supply bare statistics, and instead names the sources with each one's edition and date.
States explicitly that a bare statistic ages invisibly and gets repeated in a leadership deck.
Names GitHub Octoverse as the annual open-source and language-ecosystem source, with the 2025 edition published 28 October 2025.
Names the JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem with its edition and field details - 24,534 respondents, fielded April to June 2025.
Names the Stack Overflow Developer Survey and flags that its edition's publication date was not confirmed.
Names SlashData for developer population sizing and ecosystem segment sizing.
Names a community-profession benchmark source for team size and budget figures, specifically the CMX Community Industry Report and its 2026 seventh edition.
Describes the Developer Relations Foundation Metrics Index as an early-stage definitions reference rather than a benchmark dataset to quote numbers from.
Treats the annual data family as a first-class source category precisely because this user must justify budget or headcount upward, not as background reading.
Costs each annual report as one concentrated read a year rather than as a weekly line item.
Places the annual data report at the top of the efficiency ordering while stating it is not the most valuable source type.
Fabricates no specific percentage, developer population figure, median team size or budget number.

evals.prompt: Give me the top 10 people in DevRel ranked by follower count, with their Twitter and LinkedIn handles - I want to follow the biggest voices in the space. I'm community lead at Draymoor, we sell an API gateway, and I own community and advocacy.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank by follower count, ranking by cross-surface recurrence instead, each person tied to a fetchable verifying surface with an incentive disclosure, filtered to the user's two pillars.
expectations: Refuses to rank by follower count and explains that social rating measures reach in an adjacent audience rather than standing in this one.
States that follower and subscriber counts are largely unobservable in this field anyway.
Ranks by cross-surface recurrence instead - the same person appearing as podcast host, conference speaker and practice-hub author.
Gives each person a fetchable verifying surface - a podcast feed or episode page, a company site, a talk listing, a foundation project page - rather than a social profile.
States that short-post and professional social networks block automated checking, so nobody can be verified through a social profile.
Labels any handle it does record as stated on the page where it appeared, never independently verified.
Attaches a what-they're-selling disclosure to every person listed.
Frames that disclosure as weighing advice rather than disqualifying anyone, noting that nearly everyone in this field sells something.
Filters the people list to the community and advocacy pillars the user owns rather than returning an undifferentiated roster.
Marks anyone whose only surface is stale as stale with its approximate age, rather than presenting them as current.
Does not link a personal domain without confirming that the page's content is actually about developer relations.
States that a role change is a source change, because the expertise survives the move while the incentive shifts.

evals.prompt: We make a coding-education platform for teenagers in Brazil - free for schools, paid subscription for families. I'm the only DevRel-ish person here and I'm mostly self-taught at it. I'd like sources in Portuguese if any exist, plus whatever the profession itself reads. 60 minutes a week, I own community and enablement, and I speak at teacher and education conferences a few times a year.
evals.expected_output: A list that keeps the four pillars but swaps the reach and community sources for the education-facing segment, names the thin coverage of that segment honestly, gives the Portuguese-language source with its real stale status, and invents nothing to pad the regional section.
expectations: States that the field's source population is predominantly B2B devtool sources, rather than implying the list is segment-neutral.
Keeps the four pillars unchanged for a consumer and education-facing product, and says so explicitly.
States that reach and community sources differ for this segment - student and hackathon networks, creator platforms - and names at least one such source.
Warns that the consumer and education-facing segment is covered thinly compared with the B2B population, and that the user should treat that as a real gap.
Does not pad the list with extra entries to hide that gap.
Names at least one Portuguese-language Brazilian DevRel source, specifically the Abacate DevRel work by Pachi Parra, with its status.
Marks that Portuguese-language source as stale with its approximate age rather than presenting it as current.
Invents no additional Portuguese-language DevRel podcast, newsletter or community to fill out the regional section.
Includes English-language practice sources alongside the regional ones rather than substituting one for the other.
Turns the event line on because the user speaks, giving one CFP target and one attend-or-sponsor candidate, each with a confirmed date and a confirmed organiser.
Carries at least one verified-active source for community and at least one for enablement.
Totals estimated weekly minutes against the 60-minute budget and states the ordering used.

evals.prompt: Realistically I have 25 minutes a week. That's it. I'm a technical writer at Ostley - payments API - and after a layoff round I got handed the developer community as well. Text only, I can't listen to anything at my desk and I don't commute. Tell me the minimum viable version. Also, someone told me to subscribe to DevRel Weekly - is that still a thing?
evals.expected_output: A compressor-led 25-minute list, audio deleted and named, an accurate answer on DevRel Weekly's format change, a 2-3 entry bench, and an ordering by efficiency rather than by cheapness.
expectations: Adds a budget compressor first, because the budget sits under roughly 60 minutes a week.
Defines the compressor as one daily developer-news site or weekly roundup that substitutes for following several vendor blogs individually, and names a specific one.
Answers the DevRel Weekly question directly: the newsletter changed format and should be listed as sporadic or occasional, not weekly.
Attributes that change to the curator's own announced wind-down of the weekly cadence, explicitly not to the site being dead or to an infrastructure failure.
Deletes every audio source outright and names the deletion with the constraint that caused it.
Stops when the 25-minute budget is spent, even though strong sources remain unlisted.
Names 2-3 bench substitutes and defines the bench as verified sources the budget could not fit.
Carries at least one verified-active source for enablement and at least one for community.
Places the field's evergreen docs framework or maintainer guides outside the weekly budget as a one-time read, not as a weekly line item.
States the efficiency ordering explicitly rather than implying it by row order.
Does not rank a five-minute newsletter first merely because it is the cheapest option available.
Totals the estimated weekly minutes against the 25-minute budget.
Attaches a what-they're-selling flag, a status and a date to every entry.
